title: Where Does Food Energy Begin?

opener.title: Where Does Food Energy Begin?
opener.question: Your lunch gave you energy to run and think. But where did that energy start before it ever reached your plate?
opener.alt: An opening film that starts on the Sun, then follows its light to Earth, to Florida seen from space, to a sunny lawn, to blades of grass, and finally to the green cells inside a leaf.

frames.label: The Sun, seen by a NASA spacecraft
frames.line: The Sun sends out light in every direction, every second of every day.

frames.label: Earth, from a million miles away
frames.line: About eight minutes later, a tiny part of that light reaches Earth.

frames.label: Florida, seen from space
frames.line: It lands on oceans, cities, and forests.

frames.label: St. Augustine grass, up close
frames.line: Every blade of grass is catching it.

frames.label: Inside a leaf, under a microscope
frames.line: These green dots, called chloroplasts, catch the light and use its energy to make food.

k-warmup.text: Pick one meal: the burger, the pizza, or the apple. Do you think its energy rewinds all the way back to the sun? If yes, how many steps back? Save your prediction, then write one reason. You will check it in Part 4.

k-words.text: Sunlight. Producer. Consumer. Energy. Food chain. Photosynthesis.

k-part1.text: This page was printed in seventeen seventy-nine by Jan Ingenhousz. Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English. Then drag the sun to bright sun, to shade, and to night. Count the bubbles each time, and look at your table.

k-quiz.text: Three quick questions, just for you. They are not graded. Tap an answer and read the note under it. Each one asks you to trace energy back to where it started.

k-assign.text: Now add your page to the chain. Answer the two Part B questions about the backyard. In Part C, write your notebook page. Then tap evidence cards in the planner to build your C-E-R about where food energy begins.

wordlens.intro: Tap a word to see what it means.

words.def: Light energy from the Sun. The starting point for almost all food energy on Earth.
A living thing that makes its own food using sunlight. Plants are producers.
A living thing that eats other living things to get energy. Animals are consumers.
The ability to make things happen. Food gives your body energy to move and grow.
The path that food energy takes. Sun → plant → animal → animal that eats it.
The process plants use to turn sunlight, air, and water into food. The word means "making with light."

source.title: Jan Ingenhousz's own words
source.alt: Two printed pages from 1779, pages 5 and 6, in old-style type where the letter s often looks like an f. They describe air bubbles on leaves under water.
source.intro: In the summer of 1779, Jan Ingenhousz, a doctor born in the Netherlands, put leaves into jars of water near London and watched them closely. His book came out that same year. Before him, a scientist named Charles Bonnet had a different idea about the bubbles. Old printers used a long s that looks like an f, so “fun-fhine” means sunshine.
job: Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English.
Then find the two lines in the hunts.

lines.en: Mr. Bonnet thought the warm sun just puffed up air stuck to the leaves into bubbles, and that the cold night stopped them.
I worked hard to find out what really makes these bubbles. I think they matter much more than Mr. Bonnet imagined. Here is what I found.
Most leaves gather these bubbles on their surface when you put them under water in the sunshine, or outdoors in the daytime.
The bubbles are not made by the warm sun. Many leaves make them almost as soon as they go under water, even when the water is very cold.
The bubbles do not appear after sunset, or only a very few do.

asks.q: Hunt 1: Find the line that says WHEN leaves make bubbles.
asks.yes: Yes. In the sunshine, or outdoors in the daytime.
asks.no: That line is about something else. Look for the line that names the sunshine.

asks.q: Hunt 2: Find the line that proves the bubbles are NOT made by the warm sun.
asks.yes: Yes. Leaves made bubbles even in very cold water, so warmth is not the cause.
asks.no: Not that one. Look on the right-hand page for very cold water.

source.credit: Source: Jan Ingenhousz, Experiments upon Vegetables (London, 1779), pages 5 and 6. Scan of the Smithsonian Libraries copy, Internet Archive (public domain). Plain-English version written for this lesson.

lamp.title: Bright sun, shade, night
lamp.intro: This is a real photo of a seaweed in a jar of water, sitting in sunlight. The silver dots on it are real bubbles, like the ones Ingenhousz watched on his leaves.
job: Drag the sun to Bright sun. Tap Count.
Drag it to Shade. Count again.
Drag it to Night. Count one more time.
lamp.alt: A glass jar of water with a reddish-brown seaweed inside. Sunlight shines through the glass, and small silver bubbles cling to the seaweed.
lamp.q: Look at your table. What does the leaf need to make bubbles?

opts.hint: Ingenhousz saw bubbles even in very cold water. Read line 4 on his page again.
Check your table. How many bubbles did you count at night?

lamp.win: Yes. The bubbles are oxygen, a gas a leaf gives off while it makes sugar. No light, no bubbles. Light gives the leaf the energy it needs to make food.
lamp.credit: Photo: Raquel Sánchez de Pedro, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0 (a red seaweed, Catenella caespitosa). The moving bubbles and the counts are a model of what Ingenhousz saw.

pour.title: Where does the energy go?
pour.intro: Energy moves down a food chain one link at a time. Watch what happens to it at every link.
job: Press and hold the pour button until the grass is full. You can also tap it a few times.
Then name the kind of energy at each step.

predict.q: Say the grass in a backyard stores 1,000 units of energy from sunlight. How much of it ends up in the hawk?
opts: About 1,000. All of it passes along.
About 1. Almost all of it is gone.

pour.note: This is a model. In real food chains, about one tenth of the energy passes to the next link. The rest is used for moving, growing, and staying alive, and it ends up as heat.
pour.result: Only about 1 unit of the grass’s 1,000 reaches the hawk. At every link, most of the energy leaves as heat. That is why it takes so much grass to feed one hawk.
pour.tagsQ: Now name the kind of energy at each step. Tap the right word.

tags.yes: The sun sends us light energy.
tags.hint: What does the sun send that we can see?

tags.before: The grass stores it in sugar as
tags.yes: Energy stored in food is chemical energy.
tags.hint: Food holds stored energy. Which word means energy stored in food?

tags.before: The cricket eats grass and jumps. Jumping uses
tags.yes: Anything that moves has energy of motion.

tags.before: At every link, most of the energy leaves the body as
tags.yes: Living bodies give off heat all the time.
tags.hint: Think of how you feel after you run.

pour.q: Can the grass catch that heat and use it to make food again?

opts.t: Yes. The energy goes around and around in a circle.
opts.hint: Plants make food from light, not heat. Where does the grass get new energy every day?

opts.t: No. The heat spreads away. The grass needs new sunlight.

pour.win: Right. Energy flows one way: from the sun, through the chain, and away as heat. That is why life on Earth needs the sun every day.

yard.sunTitle: What if the sun went dark?

sunPredict.q: Suppose the sun stopped shining on this backyard. Who would be in trouble?
opts: Every living thing in the chain

story: First, the grass can’t make food. It turns yellow and stops growing.
Then the crickets run out of grass to eat.
Then the anoles run out of crickets.
Last, the hawk runs out of anoles, even though it never ate a single plant.
yard.sunBack: The sun is back on. The grass can make food again, and the chain comes back to life.
yard.sunNote: This is a model. Real living things have a little stored food, so it would take some time.
rows: Warm-Up: does your meal rewind to the sun?
No sun: who is in trouble?

twist.quote: Their great power of purifying the common air in the sunshine, and of injuring it in the shade and at night.
twist.line: That is the title of Ingenhousz’s book. He proved that leaves need light. But he never said what the light gives them. In 1845, a German doctor named Robert Mayer wrote it down: plants catch the sun’s light and store it in their food as a different kind of energy. Every meal you rewound today runs on that stored sunlight.
twist.chain: 📓 The next lesson keeps page 18 going: how scientists draw the path that energy takes.

planner.title: Plan before you write
planner.intro: Tap two or more pieces of evidence to add them to your Evidence box. Then write your claim and reasoning in your own words.
cards: A leaf in water makes bubbles in bright sun, a few in shade, and none at night.
Only producers, like grass, oak trees, and algae, can make food from sunlight.
A burger rewinds to the sun: burger → cow → grass → sun.
The hawk never eats grass, but its energy started as sunlight caught by grass.
With the sun off, every link in the backyard chain was in trouble.
At every link, most of the energy leaves as heat, so only a little reaches the hawk.

Part B: questions 1 and 2, in complete sentences.
Part C: your notebook page (what the light gives the leaf, and your own rewind).
C-E-R: a claim, at least two pieces of evidence, and your reasoning about where food energy begins.

footage.title: The Sun, up close
footage.intro: A NASA spacecraft called the Solar Dynamics Observatory watches the Sun all day, every day. This clip shows a few hours on December 31, 2012, sped up. The glowing loop on the left edge is a prominence, a giant arc of hot gas.
look: Watch the loop of glowing gas lift off the left edge.
The whole surface is churning. Some bright patches are bigger than Earth.
All the energy in your lunch started out here, about 150 million kilometers away.
footage.credit: Video: “Solar Prominence Dance, December 31, 2012,” NASA/SDO (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons. Sped up 2 times and muted for this lesson.

data.title: Wolves and moose on an island
data.intro: Isle Royale is an island in Lake Superior. Moose eat the island’s plants, and wolves eat the moose. Scientists have counted both every winter since 1959.
job: Drag across the graph to read both numbers in the same year.
Find the years when the wolves almost disappeared.
data.ask: From 2011 to 2018, the wolves dropped from 16 to just 2. What did the moose do in those years?

opts.hint: Find 2011 and 2018 on the moose line. Which number is bigger?

opts.t: The moose stayed about the same
opts.hint: Drag to 2011, then to 2018, and compare the moose numbers.

data.win: Yes. With almost no wolves to eat them, the moose grew from about 515 to about 1,475. A change in one link of a food chain changes the others. In 2018, the park began bringing new wolves to the island.
data.alt: A line graph from 1959 to 2019. The moose line rises and falls between about 400 and 2,400. The wolf line rises and falls between 2 and 50. Near the end, the wolves drop to 2 while the moose climb.
data.credit: Data: Isle Royale Wolf-Moose Project, Michigan Technological University (J. Vucetich, R. Peterson, S. Hoy), winter counts 1959 to 2019, from the project’s public data file (June 2019), downloaded November 23, 2026.

cabinet.title: A leaf that caught sunlight 100 million years ago
cabinet.alt: A 3D scan of a brown rock with the print of a large leaf in it. The leaf has three to five pointed lobes and clear veins.
cabinet.text: This is a real fossil leaf from the Smithsonian. Leaves like it were found in rocks in Ellsworth County, Kansas, and first described in 1891. Those rocks formed about 100 million years ago, when dinosaurs were alive. Like the grass in a backyard, this leaf once caught sunlight and helped its tree make food. Then it fell into mud and slowly turned into stone.
cabinet.credit: 3D model: Sterculia snowii Lesquereux, fossil leaf (USNM P2698), Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Department of Paleobiology. CC0.
